review.generic: The opening detail is centred and symmetrical, and the torn pocket still reads a little like a box before the lapel registers. The pot, flames and logs in FIG. 2 are stock-icon simple next to the magnetron. The Radarange arrives by a plain stroke draw-on. Captions are centred italics in a fixed band: tidy, not inventive.
review.exceptional: The cutaway is the thesis: microwaves cook from inside, so the film only looks inside things, and heat is the single colour, blooming from cores. FIG. 2 against FIG. 3 (the same potato cooked outside-in by fire, then inside-out by waves) explains the physics without words. Spencer drawn in phantom line, so the waves pass through a man who 'felt nothing' while only his pocket glows. The magnetron is drawn from its real construction, with eight resonant cavities and four turning electron spokes. The egg explodes onto the lens, and a cloth wipes it off, hiding the only cut. The six-foot Radarange collapses, its dimension line counting down, into a countertop box that becomes one lit window in a building of kitchens. One camera over one sheet, moving along leader lines.
review.remove: Next time: drop the second leader line and the floor clutter under the bench in the wide shot, and give FIG. 2 the same construction care as the magnetron (iron grain, real burner) or cut it to the potato alone. The OriginCtx label helper (labels that fade before platform UI, offset by their group) and the RMS loudness check are worth moving to the kit if a second film needs them.

review.generic: The large empty dark field between the pans and on the counter face reads as underfilled in wide shots rather than as deliberate Zurbaran darkness; the lime thread is a plain straight line; the restock drops and the sale lifts are clean but mechanical, with no human cause.
review.exceptional: One object carries the whole argument: a slip of paper outweighing 32 sacks is an impossible image that explains the problem without words; every error physically tips the beam further; after the turn the beam never moves again, so stillness is the proof; the bookend returns the opening picture level, 40 against 40, with the pointer resting on a lime tick in an engraved scale. Printed Didot slips, a pencil tag and YES/NO rubber stamps make the numbers material, not overlay.
review.remove: The damaged-goods tear and rice pour are too small to read in the wide shot: next time give damage its own push-in or cut it. The camera recoil on the hook is borderline (camera breathing only); keep it to impacts. The Canvas-2D wash under p5.brush strokes (p5.brush fills flood a dark ground) and the atlas View sprite helper should stay film-local until a second film proves them.

review.generic: 0-3 s: the 'pocket' is a heavy black bracket with a zigzag tear, so it reads as an abstract box until the 13.5 s reveal; the bottom third is empty paper. 0.3-1 s: the dashed wave fronts run straight through the caption and look like strikethrough. 4.2 s: 'Before 1945,' sits on the fire logs and two identical clocks stack in the same column. 8.5-12 s: the Fig. 3 subject is a plain dotted oval on a dish (potato? egg? roast?), placeholder geometry carrying the key before/after idea. 15.5 s and 17 s: the caption crosses Spencer's legs and the magnetron stand. 18.2 s: the popcorn kernel, a story object, is tiny and half off frame. 19.0 s: 'the machine.' sits on top of the egg inside Detail C. 20.3-21.5 s: the splat is flat clip-art blobs with a cartoon gloss highlight; the yolk in heat red-orange reads as ketchup or blood, not egg. 22.2 s: the cloth wipe is a full-frame tiled hatch pattern with diagonal bands, it reads as a fill texture, not cloth. 23 s: the pull-back has faded, half-drawn PERCY SPENCER / MAGNETRON labels, an emptied Detail C circle with a pink smudge and a dead lower third. 24.5 s: a ghost second Spencer floats at right and the caption sits in the empty Detail C circle. 27.5 s: the countertop microwave is a generic flat icon. 28.3-30 s: every window is identically lit, so the 'one lit window' payoff disappears and the hero window actually reads dimmer than the rest; the ground line overshoots the sheet border at 28.3 s; the bottom fifth of the end card is empty.
review.exceptional: The idea is right and owned: a single 1940s cutaway sheet where heat is the only colour and it always blooms from inside. The opening chocolate cross-section with its foil, pen clip and hot core is a distinctive, non-stock first frame, and the sag plus drip by 2 s is a real physical event. Fig. 2 'Outside in' vs Fig. 3 'Inside out' explains the science muted in two drawings. brief.typography: Numbers are printed matter: the software's count is printed on narrow paper slips in Didot numerals; the customer's order is pencil on a chit spiked on the counter; YES and NO are rubber-stamped across that chit. Captions are small Didot italic on the dark counter front. The closer is lettered in Didot on the counter's face like a shop sign.
brief.material: Theme night-signal: black paper ground, paper-white conte and charcoal, grey washes for iron, jute and wood, screen grain, light falling off from one motivated source. Lime appears only after the system takes over and only on truth: the centre tick of the pointer's scale and the alert bell.
brief.transitions: Moves through the one tableau: the camera travels along the beam from claim to goods and down to the counter; at the turn a gust sweeps the pile of slips off the pan; the restock drops sacks back in from above until the opening picture returns, level.
brief.sound: Foley-led: paper flutter and land for slips, iron clank and creak of the beam, stamp thumps for YES and NO, a sack tear for damaged goods, soft sack thumps for each sale and restock, one small bell for the alert. The music cuts out under 'vanished silently' and for a held breath before the beam comes level.

music.caption: solo plucked santoor and bowed double bass in a dry wooden room, sparse and hesitant at first with long gaps, a soft ticking woodblock like a balance settling, tension rises in the middle, then a steady warm resolved pulse to the end, instrumental

brief.payoff: The bookend: the same slip reading 40 now balanced by 40 real sacks, the beam dead level and perfectly still, the pointer resting on the lime centre tick: the picture that opened as an impossible lie closes as an ordinary truth.

review.generic: 0.0 s: the promised raking Zurbaran shaft from the upper left is a centred soft vignette; the image reads as a grey 3D model with a fuzzy outline filter, not conte on black paper. 0.0 s: the falling slip is three stacked ghost copies, a motion-blur artefact rather than a fluttering paper. 1.0-23 s: the left pan rests on the counter top and the 40 slip hangs off its front rim, floating over the counter, so the balance looks set on the table, not hanging. 6.2 s: 'The godown holds thirty-two' plays over an empty pan edge and a bare spike while the camera is still travelling; the sacks arrive late. 10-23 s: thirteen seconds of the same low framing (pan bottom-left, chit right) with the whole upper half a dead grey wall. 16.5-22 s: three near-identical frames of one pan and one slip (50, 50, 40 KG); the edits are tiny label swaps. 24.5 s: the slip is a blank grey box with bars, a placeholder; the damaged-goods sack is a thumbnail-sized smudge by the spike. 25.5 s: 'stock drops.' caption almost invisible. 26.5 s: the slip numerals double-print mid-flip (23 over 22). 28.0 s: caption 'On its own,' sits on top of the sacks in the pan. 29-33 s: 'Stock alert on your phone' shown as another chit on the spike, same composition as the order chit. 40.5-42 s: closer is a generic 'Follow / More business automations' CTA, not the brief's Didot shop-sign lettering of the line.
review.exceptional: The metaphor is genuinely specific and strong: one printed slip outweighing 32 sacks is an impossible, legible picture at frame 0.3 and an honest physical argument. The eight vanished bags drawn as dashed ghost outlines on top of the pyramid at 8 s is the best image in the film. The printed-matter typography (Didot RICE 40 BAGS slip, pencil ORDER chit, rubber YES then NO stamps, BAGS changing to KG) tells the error story in type alone. Lime held back until truth: the centre tick and the bell clapper, and the final level beam with 40 against 40 bookends the opening cleanly.
review.remove: 1) 0-42 s: hang the balance higher so both pans swing clear of the counter, and seat the slip inside the pan behind its rim; the hanging/floating error undermines every frame. 2) 0-3 s and throughout: build the single raking key from the upper left with real falloff and a hard shadow of the beam on the wall, and give sacks jute weave and tied necks in conte strokes instead of grey blobs with a fuzz outline. 3) 23.5-25.5 s: the turn has no visible cause; draw the link (a thread or chain from the counter spike to the slip's pan that ticks the number down as each sack lifts out) so the system is seen, not only said, and replace the blank grey box at 24.5 s with the gust actually scattering slips. 4) 10-23 s: break the held low framing; push in to the chit for YES/NO, then rise along the chain to the beam as each wrong slip lands, so the upper half is never dead and the beam visibly tips heavier with each lie. 5) 28 s: move 'On its own,' off the sacks onto the counter front. 6) 6.2 s: land on the sacks before 'thirty-two' is said. 7) 29-33 s: make the alert the bell ringing with lime, not a second chit identical to the order. 8) 40-42 s: letter 'Stock stops lying.' in Didot on the counter face as the brief planned, and fold the follow line under it small.

brief.story_core: The thing everyone brushes off is a finished design: one man looked closer at a nuisance that held on, and spent fourteen years teaching cloth to hold and let go the same way.
brief.emotion: Amused curiosity at a stubborn little seed, a quiet thrill when the microscope shows hooks catching loops, then delight when the whole world turns out to fasten the same way. The turn is the lens.
brief.hook: Frame 0: backlit cream rag paper filling the frame, and in its centre a strange black paper wedge, an eighth of a circle, its edge cut into curled hooks, casting a soft shadow. At 0.12 s a mirrored flap hinges open out of it in 3D with a paper flick; at 0.55 s and 0.95 s it unfolds again, each fold doubling it, until a full radial lace star of hooked spines sits there. No title, no big text.
brief.visual_question: What is this hooked black star being cut and unfolded, and why is every point a hook?
brief.metaphor: A folded Swiss papercut: everything symmetrical is born from a fold, and the fold line is a seam. The burr is a papercut unfolded from one wedge; the whole papercut world is two mirrored halves that, in the end, pull apart and press back together along that fold like hook and loop.
brief.world: One Swiss Scherenschnitt sheet, black silhouette paper cut and laid over glowing cream rag paper on a lightbox: alpine peaks and firs, two mirrored walkers and dogs at a burdock plant, a chain of identical paper dolls, a microscope, a herdsman jacket, all mirrored about one vertical fold.
brief.camera: One camera over one sheet. Starts at extreme scale on a single burr head, pulls back to the alpine top of the sheet, tracks down it beat by beat, dives into the burr on the microscope stage through black paper into a circular field of view, the field shrinks into a jacket button, and the last move pulls all the way back to show the entire sheet at once.
brief.motion: Puppets move like Lotte Reiniger cut-paper animation, on twos (12 fps steps, hinged limbs); paper folds hinge in real 3D with weight and a small overshoot; burrs snag and hold; the camera alone moves smoothly. Stillness before the rip.
brief.typography: Words are cut out of paper. The year 1941 is cut into a banner in the sky, the years 1942 to 1955 are cut as tiny numerals down the fold, the closer is cut out of the bottom border. Captions are narrow strips of black paper with the words cut through them (Futura), placed away from the fold.
brief.material: Theme scherenschnitt: black silhouette paper (ink) over backlit cream rag paper (bg), a warm brown cast shadow under every cut layer from a light at upper left, paper fibre grain and a lightbox falloff. The single red is the grip: the hook tips under the lens and the fastener.
brief.transitions: Pull-back from one burr to the alps; a tracking descent down the sheet for the dolls; a push through the black paper of the burr on the microscope stage opens a circular field of view; that circle shrinks and becomes a jacket button; the scissors cut down the fold while the camera pulls back to the whole sheet, which then rips apart and presses shut.

review.generic: The caption slips are still a caption track, even cut and tilted. The micro view's hooks and loops are diagrammatic, not drawn: stiff tapered stalks and evenly spaced loops, and the outer hooks fall outside the field. The Alps scene is a centred, symmetrical tableau that only moves through its walkers; the profile figures crowd each other when bent.
review.exceptional: The opening is one cut wedge of black paper that unfolds three times into a hooked burr, then the camera pulls back while the stem is cut out beneath it. The push through the burr's black core (a ring of cut holes like moons) opens into the field of view, and that circle shrinks into a jacket button that then pops off. The ending pays off the fold: scissors cut the whole symmetrical sheet down its fold, one snip a year on a paper tag, and the two halves of the world drift apart in silence, slam together, rip apart with red hooks and cream loops along the seam, and press shut for good.

brief.story_core: Paying fifteen people by hand is not one sum but hundreds of small ones, and every recheck adds more ink; the same month can run as one clean line from attendance to payslip.
brief.emotion: Pressure and low dread as the ballpoint keeps overwriting the same figures and a complaint lands on the page; relief and lightness when the tangle of rechecks is pulled taut into one line and the pen is finally capped and left still.
brief.hook: Frame 0: an extreme top-down macro of one PAY cell in a handwritten muster roll on pale ledger paper; the figure 13,800 is struck through, 13,600 is written over it, and a blue ballpoint tip rests on the cell, its trail already looping in from the left. At 0.15 s the pen scratches a third figure, 13,400, over the other two, presses so hard the ink pools; by 1 s it lifts and strikes that one through as well; from 1.2 s the camera pulls back down the column to show fifteen cells, every one overwritten, while the pen jabs a question mark beside each row. No title, no big text.
brief.visual_question: Why does someone keep rewriting the same salary figure, and which one is right?
brief.metaphor: The pen trail: every add, subtract and recheck is one more pass of the ballpoint across the register, and its trail piles up into a maze; automation is that same single line pulled taut from attendance to salary, and the pen laid down for good.
brief.world: One Indian muster roll register lying open under cool daylight: ruled ledger paper with pale blue rules and a red double margin, fifteen staff names written in blue ballpoint, a 31-day attendance grid of P, A and L marks, LEAVE, OT and PAY columns, a folded complaint chit held by a steel paper clip, a capped blue ballpoint pen with a contact shadow, and later seven filled pages laid out side by side as a week.
brief.camera: One locked top-down camera over the paper, moving like a document camera: macro on single cells, slow tracks along a row as the pen works, a pull-back to the whole page for the maze, page turns for each new month, and one long final pull-back that reveals seven pages of a week.
brief.motion: Organic, hand-made: the ballpoint writes at handwriting speed with pressure pauses, jabs and backtracks, ink appears only where the pen has been; after the turn nothing is handwritten, printed marks arrive in an even mechanical cascade and the pen lies still; one taut pull where the tangled trail straightens from both ends with weight and a small overshoot.
brief.typography: Two families: Bradley Hand for everything the person writes (names, attendance marks, overwritten sums, the circled 15, the complaint chit), ink-roughened and revealed as written; JetBrains Mono for everything the system does (printed ticks, rolling PAY figures, PAID 1st). Handwriting versus print is the before and after. Captions are small ballpoint-blue mono lines in the lower margin of the page, hidden where the page already says the words.
brief.material: Theme muster: pale cool ledger paper, ballpoint blue ink, pale blue rules, the register red only for the margin and the strike-throughs, and one printed green that means automated and paid. Soft daylight from the upper left, a contact shadow under the pen and clip, paper grain multiplied.
brief.transitions: Every change is a camera move over the same register or a physical page event: pull-backs along the column, a track along a row, the tangle pulling straight carries the eye from attendance to salary, a page turn starts the self-running month, page turns repeat for every month after, and the last pull-back reveals the week of pages.
brief.sound: Rhythmic foley from the desk only: ballpoint scratch and taps under the writing, the chit landing and the paper clip snapping, a pen click when it is capped, page flips for each month, a soft stamp for PAID; the music is cut for the beat before the line goes taut so the pull lands in silence.

review.generic: 18.0 s: the lens field shrinks into a flat clip-art four-hole button icon centred on plain black: no paper, no shadow, no grain, the one SaaS-icon frame in the film. 7.5-12.5 s: the paper dolls are rectangles with bowler hats, and the bowing row at 9 s is robotic boxes, which is placeholder geometry. The microscope at 9-12.5 s is stacked bars whose head floats with no arm joining it to the stage, and the burr on the slide is about 20 px. 19.5-24 s: the jacket is a rectangle drawn with cream outline strokes, which is vector-icon language, not cut paper, and the 'stuck zip' pockets are too small to read. 29-30.4 s: the closer pushes back in to the jacket, leaves the bottom 45 percent as an empty black band, then sets 'Follow / More backstories.' in plain type. It is a stock end card, not cut out of the border. Captions are cut into VO fragments ('walks his dog in', 'the Alps.', 'you just press and') that only repeat the voice, in a humanist sans rather than Futura, as solid strips rather than words cut through paper. At 7.5 s 'Most people just brush' loses its strip and floats on the black fir band. At 18.8-24 s every caption sits on the microscope base. 26-26.5 s: the years 1942-1955 show as one tiny paper tag at a time next to tiny scissors and are unreadable. At 26 s the scissors and the '1950' tag pile up on the microscope.
review.exceptional: 0-2.6 s: a hooked black wedge hinges open into a radial burr star and then grows into a mirrored burdock plant. It is an unusual opening and it carries the whole metaphor. 12.9 s: the push through the burr's black paper is the best frame in the film, layered cut paper with real depth and shadow. 13.5-17.4 s: the microscope field with red hook tips catching black loops is clear, specific and correctly coloured; the single red is earned. 25-26.5 s: the pull-back reveals the whole story as one symmetrical Scherenschnitt sheet. 27-28.5 s: the sheet rips down the fold with red hooks on one edge and loops on the other, hangs open on dark, and presses shut. That is the memorable moment, and it pays off the metaphor. Nothing in the studio's recent history looks like this.
review.remove: 1) 29-30.4 s: hold the full sheet after it presses shut and do not push back in to the jacket. Cut the closer out of the bottom border (cream letters through black paper) and kill the empty black band and the plain 'Follow' card. 2) 17.4-18.8 s: replace the clip-art button with a cut-paper horn button on the jacket's black paper, with grain, shadow and thread, so the lens circle lands on a real object. 3) All captions: make them strips with the words cut through (bg showing through, Futura), use whole VO clauses rather than fragments, keep a strip under the 7.5 s line, and move the 18.8-24 s captions off the microscope base into clear cream space. 4) 7.5-12.5 s: redraw the dolls as proper Reiniger silhouettes with jacket tails, hands and stride, and the bowing row with real bent figures. Join the microscope head to an arm and enlarge the burr on the slide at least 3x. 5) 19.5-24 s: draw the jacket as cut silhouette with interior cut-outs rather than outline strokes. Make the popping button and the jammed zip large enough to read, or drop the pocket zips. 6) 25.6-26.5 s: cut the years 1942-1955 as a readable column of numerals down the fold, staying on screen as they accumulate, and keep the scissors and tags clear of the microscope.

review.generic: Captions are still a strip system, though now whole sentences in Futura pinned to clear cream (or cut straight into the black lens surround and the bottom border). In the jacket beat the black bottom border fills the lower quarter of the frame; it carries the caption but is otherwise plain. The felt texture at the 26x button close-up reads as tweed blotches rather than fine wool. The micro hooks and loops are still more diagram than drawing. The year tag is a counter riding the scissors, not a column of numerals cut down the fold; it is legible now (about 50 px) and passes clear of the microscope, but the middle years flick by.
review.exceptional: The lens closes onto a real cut-paper button: two layers of card lit from the upper left, a pressed dish, punched holes, a linen thread cross, and placket stitching cut into felt-textured wool around it. The closer holds the whole symmetrical sheet after it presses shut: 'Follow' is knifed out of the bottom border, each letter's black piece lifts and drops away, and the scissors lie on the wooden worktable below with their tag reading 1955. Puppets are now built from their parts (breeches with a cut knee band, calves, heeled boots, fitted coats with cut buttons, profile heads with Alpine hats), the microscope is a real side-on instrument (horseshoe foot, tilt joint, curved limb, focus knob, stage clips, mirror), and the burr on its slide is about 3x larger.

review.generic: The pen moves with no hand, so it reads as a puppet more than a person working. Bradley Hand is still recognisably a font even with per-glyph jitter. The week sheets' scribble is smooth arcs, not the jagged rechecking route of the first page. The pay figures rolling like a counter is a familiar motion-graphics device. In the closer, the lower 40 percent of the frame is empty desk.
review.exceptional: The pen's real route builds the maze: every recheck we watched is on the page, and the same line is pulled taut from day 1 to the total, then turns green. Handwriting against print carries before and after without a single label. The PAID 1 NOV stamp lands where the complaint chit lay. Frame 0 and the 'no mistakes' beat are the same macro of Raju's cell, overwritten and then clean. The capped pen lies still on the desk for the rest of the film. The salary day is buried under seven loose handwritten sheets, Monday to Sunday.
review.remove: The ballpoint question-mark jabs down the column could be half as many. The quick DEC and JAN pages flip by too fast to read and could be one flip. Next time give the pen a hand shadow, or move it by touch only. A per-glyph handwriting helper is a kit candidate only after a second film proves it.

brief.story_core: The thing everyone brushes off is a finished design: one man looked closer at a nuisance that held on, and spent fourteen years teaching cloth to hold and let go the same way.
brief.emotion: Amused curiosity at a stubborn little seed, a quiet thrill when the microscope shows hooks catching loops, then delight when the whole world turns out to fasten the same way. The turn is the lens.
brief.hook: Frame 0: backlit cream rag paper filling the frame, and in its centre a strange black paper wedge, an eighth of a circle, its edge cut into curled hooks, casting a soft shadow. At 0.12 s a mirrored flap hinges open out of it in 3D with a paper flick; at 0.55 s and 0.95 s it unfolds again, each fold doubling it, until a full radial lace star of hooked spines sits there. No title, no big text.
brief.visual_question: What is this hooked black star being cut and unfolded, and why is every point a hook?
brief.metaphor: A folded Swiss papercut: everything symmetrical is born from a fold, and the fold line is a seam. The burr is a papercut unfolded from one wedge; the whole papercut world is two mirrored halves that, in the end, pull apart and press back together along that fold like hook and loop.
brief.world: One Swiss Scherenschnitt sheet, black silhouette paper cut and laid over glowing cream rag paper on a lightbox: alpine peaks and firs, two mirrored walkers and dogs at a burdock plant, a chain of identical paper dolls, a microscope, a herdsman jacket, all mirrored about one vertical fold.
brief.camera: One camera over one sheet. Starts at extreme scale on a single burr head, pulls back to the alpine top of the sheet, tracks down it beat by beat, dives into the burr on the microscope stage through black paper into a circular field of view, the field shrinks into a jacket button, and the last move pulls all the way back to show the entire sheet at once.
brief.motion: Puppets move like Lotte Reiniger cut-paper animation, on twos (12 fps steps, hinged limbs); paper folds hinge in real 3D with weight and a small overshoot; burrs snag and hold; the camera alone moves smoothly. Stillness before the rip.
brief.typography: Words are cut out of paper. The year 1941 is cut into a banner in the sky, the years 1942 to 1955 are cut as tiny numerals down the fold, the closer is cut out of the bottom border. Captions are narrow strips of black paper with the words cut through them (Futura), placed away from the fold.
brief.material: Theme scherenschnitt: black silhouette paper (ink) over backlit cream rag paper (bg), a warm brown cast shadow under every cut layer from a light at upper left, paper fibre grain and a lightbox falloff. The single red is the grip: the hook tips under the lens and the fastener.
brief.transitions: Pull-back from one burr to the alps; a tracking descent down the sheet for the dolls; a push through the black paper of the burr on the microscope stage opens a circular field of view; that circle shrinks and becomes a jacket button; the scissors cut down the fold while the camera pulls back to the whole sheet, which then rips apart and presses shut.
brief.sound: Paper flicks for each unfold, soft taps as burrs snag, a cloth swish for the brushing dolls, glass for the slide, a button pop and a metal jam for the zip, a heavy press and a cloth tear for press and pull, a scissor snip per year down the fold, silence before the whole sheet rips apart, then one press as it sticks back.

review.generic: 3.0-10.0 s: the walkers, dogs and doll chain are blocky rectangle-torso puppets with ball heads, nowhere near the lace detail of real Scherenschnitt or Reiniger; the hook promised fine cutwork and the people are clip-art. 0.0 s: the wedge reads as three walking-stick handles more than a burr segment. 11.5 s and 24.6-30 s: two concentric-heart ornaments float beside the microscope with no cause, pure filler. 18.1 s: the button macro is a flat plastic disc on noise texture, a stock 'cosy' still. 18.6-25 s: the jacket is a flat rectangle with sleeves held ~6 s in the same centred composition, with the lower quarter of the frame a dead dark band that only exists to carry a caption. Every caption is the VO verbatim on a plain black subtitle bar (not words cut through paper as briefed). 13.0 s: the push through the burr's holes reads as moon phases, not paper. 29.5 s: closer resolves to a generic 'Follow / More backstories' CTA.
review.exceptional: 0.0-2.0 s: the wedge hinging out into a radial hooked star that then grows a stem and becomes the burdock plant is a genuinely unseen opening and plants the fold metaphor in two seconds. 14.2-17.5 s: the circular lens field with red hook tips catching black loops is the clearest and best-drawn image in the film, and the single red is earned. 25.6-26.4 s: the scissors cutting down the fold with 1944/1948/1952/1955 tags dangling, and 26.9 s the whole sheet ripping into a red-hook edge and a cream-loop edge over the wood table, then pressing shut at 27.2 s, is a real memorable payoff that makes the whole film one object.
review.remove: 1) 3.0-12.5 s: redraw the walkers, dogs and doll chain as proper cutwork silhouettes (lace boots, hat feathers, fur fringe, fingers, staff knots) at the density of the burr star; they carry the story and are the crudest objects on screen. 2) 18.6-25 s: kill the dead dark band; make the jacket a cut-paper Swiss herdsman jacket with lace trim, frame it tighter or move the camera during the button fumble and zip jam, and show the stuck zip clearly (it is invisible at 21 s); captions as strips cut into the paper above the hem. 3) All captions: replace verbatim VO bars with shorter cut-paper words that add information (e.g. 'he looked closer', '14 years'), cut through black strips as briefed. 4) 26.9 s: hold the ripped-open sheet at least 0.6 s in stillness before the press so the hook/loop seam registers. 5) 11.5 s and 24.6 s on: remove the floating hearts or mirror the microscope so the closing sheet is truly symmetrical about the fold. 6) 0.0 s: give the wedge burr bracts (a cupped base and many short hooked spines) so frame 0 reads as a seed, not walking sticks. 7) 29.5 s: cut the closer out of the bottom border as a line of the story, not 'Follow'.

review.generic: The microscope is still an asymmetric object sitting on the fold of an otherwise mirrored sheet. The iris-to-button handoff at 18 s is still a fairly plain cream disc. Captions are still one strip at a time in a single face; the cut-letter shadow is subtle at phone size.
review.exceptional: Frame 0 now reads as a burr cupule: a scalloped cup pierced with pointed scales and thirteen tapering bracts ending in tiny hooks; it unfolds into a pierced rosette. The walkers, dogs and doll chain are real cutwork: laced boots, patterned stockings, garters with tassels, feather sprays with barbs, a pipe with a smoke curl, a rucksack with a bedroll, fingers, an alpenstock bound with knots, a Bernese dog with a fur fringe, plumed tail, collar and bell. The jacket is a herdsman's jacket with lace hem, cuffs, eyelet yoke, edelweiss and a lace column, framed tight; the camera pushes into the straining button and down to the zip, which visibly jams on a tuck of lining and is tugged twice. Captions are short words cut through black strips that add facts the voice leaves out (born 1907, burdock seed heads, nobody kept one, he looked closer, every spine ends in a hook, seeds ride away on fur, velours + crochet = Velcro). The torn sheet now hangs open and still for about 0.65 s in silence before it presses shut. The closer cuts a line of the story, 'look closer.', out of the bottom border, the platform line under it.
review.remove: Cut-paper helpers (Limb, Hand, tufts, the cut-through caption strip) are candidates for the kit only if a second film proves them. Next time give the microscope a mirrored twin or put it off the fold from the start.

review.generic: 0.0 s: the wedge is small (about a third of the width) and centred in a sea of flat cream, so frame 0 reads as a logo on a blank card rather than a strange object. 2.0 s: the top 35% is empty cream under a crude band of black triangles. 3.0-6.3 s: the alps/walkers composition is held almost unchanged for over 3 s, only the caption strip swaps, and the burrs snagging on the dogs are a few pixels wide, so the inciting event barely reads. 8-10 s: the dolls' brushing gesture is tiny, and the hero's burr is a dot. 12 s: the burr on the microscope stage is a speck. 13.0 s: a fully black, empty frame during the push into the lens (a dead beat, not a cut through paper). 14 s: the red hooks hang above the loops instead of visibly snagging them. 17.5 s: the field of view washes out with no event. 24 s: the 'velours + crochet = Velcro' strip sits on top of the diamond ornament line. 25.5 s and 26 s: the year tags (1945, 1952) are pasted over the walkers and the jacket chest instead of cut as small numerals down the fold as briefed, and a black blob sits on the jacket at 26 s. 26.5 s: during the rip the microscope halves don't mirror and look broken. 28.5-30.4 s: the whole closer shows a sheet whose figures are tiny on a phone, with the bottom quarter dead wood grain holding only scissors and a tag.
review.exceptional: One coherent, authored world: a real Scherenschnitt sheet with cast shadows, lightbox falloff and Futura captions cut into black strips. The hook unfolding a hooked wedge into a radial burr (0-1 s) and then growing it into a burdock plant is specific and not a common opening. Red used only as grip (hook tips under the lens, the jacket seam) is disciplined. The circle of the lens becoming a button and then the button popping off the jacket is a clean, caused transition. The payoff, the entire sheet ripping down its fold with red hooks on one edge and white loops on the other and then pressing shut, is a genuinely memorable, story-specific metaphor, and the closer letters falling out of the bottom border as paper cut-outs is a nice touch.
review.remove: 1) 13.0 s: kill the all-black frame; push through the burr's black paper so the lens circle opens while paper is still on screen (no empty black beat). 2) 3.0-6.3 s: break the held composition; push in on the dogs as the burrs hook into fur, making the burrs large enough to read (at least 1/8 frame width), and cut the caption swap to the snag. 3) 25.5-26.5 s: move the year tags off the walkers and jacket; cut 1942-1955 as small numerals running down the fold line, as briefed. 4) 28.5-30.4 s: crop the closer tighter so the sheet fills about 90% of the frame; remove the dead wood band at the bottom or move scissors and the 1955 tag into the sheet's margin. 5) 0.0 s: scale the wedge up to about 55% of the width and give it a harder cast shadow so frame 0 is an object, not an icon. 6) 14-15 s: show the hooks actually catching loops and tugging them (a visible pull), not hovering above. 7) 24 s: move the 'velours + crochet = Velcro' strip off the ornament line. 8) 26.5 s: mirror the microscope about the fold so the rip splits a symmetrical object cleanly. 9) 12 s: make the burr on the microscope stage large enough to read before the dive.

review.generic: Still weaker spots: the button swap at about 17.5 s fades rather than happening as an event; at 24 s the microscope is cropped at the top of the frame; the fallen closer letters partly pile on each other on the margin; the year numerals carry a cream halo that reads slightly like a label over the jacket.
review.exceptional: Frame 0 is now a big folded wedge with a hard lamp shadow. The camera pushes in on the dog as burrs the size of an eighth of the frame hook into its fur, and the caption is cut on the snag. The dive no longer blacks out: the burr fills the frame and the lens opens inside its black cup while paper is still on screen. Under the lens, hooks go behind the loops, catch them in the crook (each point passes over its loop) and drag them up. The microscope is now a symmetric lyre that the rip splits into true halves. The years 1942 to 1955 are cut small down the fold, one per snip. The closer holds the sheet filling the width, with its paper margin running off the bottom, where the scissors and the cut-out letters land.
review.remove: Next time, avoid tying a label to a moving prop (the year tag) and check every frame of the closing shot for dead table. The lens-opens-in-the-object transition and the paper margin for the cut-offs are film-specific helpers, not kit material yet.

brief.emotion: Amused curiosity at a stubborn little seed, a quiet thrill when the microscope shows hooks catching loops, then delight when the whole world turns out to fasten the same way. The turn is the lens.
brief.hook: Frame 0: backlit cream rag paper filling the frame, and in its centre a strange black paper wedge, an eighth of a circle, its edge cut into curled hooks, casting a soft shadow. At 0.12 s a mirrored flap hinges open out of it in 3D with a paper flick; at 0.55 s and 0.95 s it unfolds again, each fold doubling it, until a full radial lace star of hooked spines sits there. No title, no big text.
brief.visual_question: What is this hooked black star being cut and unfolded, and why is every point a hook?

brief.world: One Swiss Scherenschnitt sheet, black silhouette paper cut and laid over glowing cream rag paper on a lightbox: alpine peaks and firs, two mirrored walkers and dogs at a burdock plant, a chain of identical paper dolls, a microscope, a herdsman jacket, all mirrored about one vertical fold.
brief.camera: One camera over one sheet. Starts at extreme scale on a single burr head, pulls back to the alpine top of the sheet, tracks down it beat by beat, dives into the burr on the microscope stage through black paper into a circular field of view, the field shrinks into a jacket button, and the last move pulls all the way back to show the entire sheet at once.

review.generic: Dead frame area keeps coming back: at 7.2 s the bottom half is empty cream between the walker row and a lone dotted rule; at 14 to 17.6 s the lower third is flat black under the lens; at 22.4 to 25 s the bottom 30% is a blank black band under the jacket; at 28.5 s the bottom quarter is bare paper with a small pair of scissors. The microscope (8.5 to 13 s) reads as an arbor press or a robot face (two cog 'eyes', a nozzle 'nose'), and at 12.8 s it fills the frame while the burr on the stage is tiny. The button at 17.8 s is a flat, generic vector disc floating in black, the only object in the film that is not cut paper. Walker faces (6 s) are crude blobs with a slot eye. At 1.0 s the finished star shrinks to a small mark in a big empty frame, and by 1.6 s it is already a plant, so the mystery is answered almost before it lands. The cut numerals 1942 to 1955 down the fold (25.5 to 30 s) are about 9 px tall and unreadable on a phone. Composition held too long: the lens from 13.0 to 17.6 s (4.5 s), the 1941 walkers from 3.0 to 5 s, the jacket from 22.4 to 25 s.
review.exceptional: The 0 to 1 s hinged papercut fold-out of the hooked wedge is an opening I have not seen. The push at 13.2 s through the black paper spines of the burr, with 3D cut spines splaying around the circle and the red hooks already visible inside, is real cinematography. The odd-one-out doll in a jacket holding up the burr ('nobody kept one', 10 s) tells the story with no words. The pull-back at 25.5 s that turns the whole film into one framed Scherenschnitt sheet, then the fold ripping open as red hooks and white loops at 26.6 s, is the memorable moment and pays the metaphor off exactly. 'look closer.' cut from the bottom border with its letter offcuts lying under the scissors is an authored closer.
review.remove: 1) 22.4 to 25 s and 14 to 17.6 s: kill the dead bands. Frame the jacket larger (to about 75% of the height) so the black scalloped ground takes no more than 10%, and push in on the lens so the circle fills about 85% of the width, or put the hooked loops' catch high in the frame and move the caption strip into the gap. 2) 8.5 to 13 s: redraw the microscope as an unmistakable 1940s brass microscope silhouette (eyepiece tube, angled arm, objective turret, stage clips, mirror) with no face-like cog pairs; make the burr on the stage at least 3 times larger at 12.8 s. 3) 13.0 to 17.6 s: cut the lens hold to 2.5 s or give it a second beat (a hook pulls one loop taut and the fabric jerks); 17.8 s: make the button a cut-paper disc with a cast shadow and grain like everything else. 4) 7.2 s: tighten the camera descent so the empty band between walkers and dolls never fills half the frame. 5) 1.0 to 1.6 s: hold the full star larger (about 70% of width) for 0.4 s before the pull-back reveals the plant. 6) 25.5 to 30 s: cut the year numerals at least 3 times larger, or drop the ones that cannot be read. 7) 28.5 s: lift the sheet so the closer and offcuts sit in the lower third instead of bare paper.

brief.story_core: Paying fifteen people by hand is not one sum but hundreds of small ones, and every recheck adds more ink; the same month can run as one clean line from attendance to payslip.
brief.emotion: Pressure and low dread as the ballpoint keeps overwriting the same figures and a complaint lands on the page; relief and lightness when the tangle of rechecks is pulled taut into one line and the pen is finally capped and left still.
brief.hook: Frame 0: an extreme top-down macro of one PAY cell in a handwritten muster roll on pale ledger paper, a blue ballpoint resting in it: 13,800 is struck through and 13,600 is written over it, and the pay date above reads 1st and 5th struck out, then 7th. At 0.15 s the pen writes a third figure, 13,400, under the other two; at 0.95 s it strikes 13,600 through and jabs a question mark beside the cell; from 1.2 s the camera pulls back down the column to show fifteen cells, every one overwritten, while the pen jabs a question mark beside each row. No title, no big text.
brief.visual_question: Why does someone keep rewriting the same salary figure, and which one is right?
brief.metaphor: The pen trail: every add, subtract and recheck is one more pass of the ballpoint across the register, and its trail piles up into a maze; automation is that same single line pulled taut from attendance to salary, and the pen laid down for good.
brief.world: One Indian muster roll register lying open under cool daylight: ruled ledger paper with pale blue rules and a red double margin, fifteen staff names written in blue ballpoint, a 31-day attendance grid of P, A and L marks, LEAVE, OT and PAY columns, a folded complaint chit held by a steel paper clip, a capped blue ballpoint pen with a contact shadow, and at the end seven loose handwritten pages, Monday to Sunday, dropped one on another as a week.
brief.camera: One locked top-down camera over the paper, moving like a document camera: macro on single cells, slow tracks along a row as the pen works, a pull-back to the whole page for the maze, page turns for each new month, and one long final pull-back that reveals seven pages of a week.
brief.motion: Organic, hand-made: the ballpoint writes at handwriting speed with pressure pauses, jabs and backtracks, ink appears only where the pen has been; after the turn nothing is handwritten, printed marks arrive in an even mechanical cascade and the pen lies still; one taut pull where the tangled trail straightens from both ends with weight and a small overshoot.
brief.typography: Two families: Bradley Hand for everything the person writes (names, attendance marks, overwritten sums, the circled 15, the complaint chit), ink-roughened and revealed as written; JetBrains Mono for everything the system does (printed ticks, rolling PAY figures, PAID 1st). Handwriting versus print is the before and after. Captions are small ballpoint-blue mono lines in the lower margin of the page, hidden where the page already says the words.
brief.material: Theme muster: pale cool ledger paper, ballpoint blue ink, pale blue rules, the register red only for the margin and the strike-throughs, and one printed green that means automated and paid. Soft daylight from the upper left, a contact shadow under the pen and clip, paper grain multiplied.
brief.transitions: Every change is a camera move over the same register or a physical page event: pull-backs along the column, a track along a row, the tangle pulling straight carries the eye from attendance to salary, a page turn starts the self-running month, page turns repeat for every month after, and the last pull-back reveals the week of pages.
brief.sound: Rhythmic foley from the desk only: ballpoint scratch and taps under the writing, the chit landing and the paper clip snapping, a pen click when it is capped, page flips for each month, a soft stamp for PAID; the music is cut for the beat before the line goes taut so the pull lands in silence.

review.generic: Bradley Hand still reads as a typeface in the big figures despite per-glyph lean, drift and spacing. The hand is only a soft cast shadow; in the wide maze shot the pen works at the page's right edge, so most of the shadow falls on the dark desk and the pen still reads lightly held there. The closer keeps a desk band of about a fifth of the frame, holding the capped pen. Sound is unchanged apart from fewer pen taps.
review.exceptional: The pen now sits at a right hand's writing angle, its barrel toward the writer, with a soft hand-and-forearm shadow that sweeps across the rows during the rechecks. The shadow leaves once the pen is laid down, so the stillness after the turn is a person who has stopped working. The pen's real route still builds the maze and is pulled taut into the green line. The week sheets carry the same jagged rechecking route as October. Pay figures are struck whole down the column like a print head. One readable DEC page and PAID 1 DEC replace the two unreadable flips.
review.remove: Halve the hook's question-mark jabs (done: 8 of 15 rows). Fold the DEC and JAN flips into one readable month (done). Next time: a real top-down hand instead of a shadow if the tooling allows. Do not use a font for handwriting; write it with per-stroke paths. Per-glyph handwriting and the hand shadow are kit candidates only after a second film proves them. Give the closer a composition without a desk band.

review.generic: 0.0-1.0 s: grey semicircle loops float above 13,800 and look like a render glitch, not ink. 3.0 s onward: the 'maze' is sine and zigzag waves with an even period running along each row (15.5-19.6 s). It reads like seismograph noise or a CSS squiggle, not ballpoint rechecking. 20.4 s: the payoff is a 2 px green diagonal from Raju's first P to the bottom-right of TOTAL. A single diagonal stroke across a register page means 'cancelled' or 'void', and it then stays on every printed page (22.5, 23.5, 25, 35.5, 37, 43.8 s), striking through 14,100, 11,250 and the ticks. It never meets the ATTENDANCE IN or SALARY OUT the brief promised. Dead frame: a flat navy band fills the top 20-40% at 4.5-6.5 s, 13-15.5 s, 27-30 s and 38.5 s, where the page is pushed into the right half. The lower third of the page is empty paper at 17-22 s and 37 s. Captions sit on key figures: 1.0 s over 12,300; 3.0 s over row 11 DAYS; 21.2 s over Arjun and TOTAL; 30-33.5 s over 11,800 and its tick; 38.5 s over 11,800. 25 s: the payslips are small grey tag chips that cover the first digit of 13,400 and are clipped at the page edge, like a SaaS toast, not a WhatsApp payslip. 43.8 s: a stock 'Follow / More business automations' end card in big mono with a green rule, and an empty navy bottom fifth. No paper clip on the chit (4.5-13 s); it is a flat rectangle with a fold line.
review.exceptional: The opening macro is authored and specific: struck-through 1st/5th/7th, 13,800 to 13,600 to 13,400 overwritten at handwriting speed by a well-lit ballpoint with a contact shadow, then question marks running down the column on a looping trail (0-3 s). This is unlike anything in the studio's history. Handwriting against print carries the before and after with no explanation. The rhyme at 31.5-33.5 s, the same PAY cell in the same macro framing now in clean mono with green ticks under a hand-inked PAID 1 NOV stamp, is the best shot in the film. The pen is laid off the page onto the desk at 21.2 s and stays there, which is a quiet, earned gesture. The week of seven handwritten sheets (Thu, Sun) piling up at 39.8-42.3 s is a strong, specific image.
review.remove: 1) 19.6-21.2 s: redraw the payoff. Pull the tangle taut into a thick, weighted green ink line that runs along one row from the attendance grid to the PAY column, so it reads as a path and not a diagonal cancel stroke. Remove it from every printed page after the turn (22.5-43.8 s) so it never strikes through figures. 2) 38.5-43.8 s: fix the order. The myth beat buries the green page under handwritten sheets, then the closer jumps back to the clean Dec page with a stock 'Follow' card, so without captions it reads as 'automation failed, back to hand maths'. Either move the week-of-pages reveal before the turn (as the cost of manual) or end on the buried green page. Replace the Follow card with an end mark in the film's own language, such as a stamp or a printed line in the margin. 3) 4.5-6.5 s, 13-15.5 s, 27-30 s, 38.5 s: reframe so the paper fills the frame. No flat navy bands over 10% of height, and no page shoved into the right half. Crop out the empty lower third of the page at 17-22 s and 37 s. 4) 3-19.6 s: draw the maze as ballpoint retracing (uneven loops, backtracks, pressure-varied overlapping passes between DAYS, LEAVE, OT and PAY cells) instead of evenly periodic sine and zigzag waves. 5) Captions: move the strip into the lower page margin as the brief asks. Never place it over a figure (1.0, 3.0, 21.2, 30-33.5, 38.5 s). Drop captions where the page already shows the words, such as 'Fifteen people paid right' over the ticks at 27 s. 6) 25 s: make the payslips real slips, small printed paper chits sliding out from each PAY row, and keep them clear of the figures and inside the frame. 7) 0-1 s: remove the floating grey semicircle loops above 13,800. 8) 4.5 s: add the steel paper clip with a contact shadow, and let the chit land with weight.

review.generic: Sound is unchanged from the failed cut: correct desk foley, but no moment where sound carries the story on its own. Transitions are camera moves and two page turns, competent, not inventive. The payslips still cross PAY figures for a fraction of a second in flight. The wide shot at 21.2 s, as the camera settles, still shows a band of empty lower margin.
review.exceptional: The opening macro (struck dates, 13,800 to 13,600 to 13,400 at handwriting speed) and the PAY-cell rhyme under the PAID 1 NOV stamp are kept. The payoff now reads as a path: the maze, drawn as hurried leaning loops, scratches and doubled-back passes with pressure runs, is pulled taut into a heavy green underline along Raju's row from his first day of attendance to his pay, while the printed ATTENDANCE and PAY headings re-ink green. The line lives only on the October page. The ending: seven handwritten sheets (Mon to Sun) slap down beside the printed December PAY column with its ticks and stamp, and the closer is printed in that page's margin with the same green tick. Captions are printed lines in the page's lower margin or under the title, hidden wherever a figure would sit beneath them. A camera clamp keeps paper in frame, so there are no navy bands. The clamp, scrawl() and the margin-anchored caption placement could go into the kit if a second film needs them.
review.remove: Payslip flights over the figures (launch them from the margin side next time). The hand-shadow forearm still shows as a soft grey shape at the right edge in wide shots.

brief.story_core: The same sealed pocket of air was useless on a wall and priceless around a machine: an invention failed twice not because it was bad but because it was hung in the wrong place.
brief.emotion: Amused pity for two men whose wallpaper cannot even hold a calendar, mild deflation as it fails again in a greenhouse, then a jolt of delight when the same wrap takes a full drop and the computer inside keeps turning; the turn is the drop.
brief.hook: Frame 0: a close view of a 1957 living-room wall papered in glossy teal domes, a printed 1957 calendar hanging from a nail driven straight through one dome, the dome dimpled and straining around the nail. At 0.15 s the dome pops, the nail tips out and the calendar drops, see-sawing like falling paper, and lands on the floorboards by 1 s while the camera starts to pull back. No title, no big text.
brief.visual_question: What kind of wall pops, and who papered a room with it?
brief.metaphor: Bubble wrap as the wrong wallpaper: one sheet of sealed air travels from a wall that cannot hold a nail, through a roller where it is born, past a shop and a greenhouse that reject it, to the one place it belongs, hugging a computer as it falls.
brief.world: A 1957 magazine illustration printed in two inks on newsprint: flat cut-paper shapes with ink keylines, teal Ben-Day dots for shade, one coral plate slightly out of register; a living room, a workshop roller mangle, a wallpaper display rack, a backyard greenhouse and a loading dock with an IBM tape drive.
brief.camera: A tracking camera that follows the sheet itself: close on the nail, pull back to the room, push into the flopped strip, tilt down the roller as the sheet comes out, ride the lone roll into the greenhouse, take the torn sheet across the lens to the dock, hold locked for the drop, dive into a single bubble and pull back to the room where it started.
brief.motion: Gravity and air: paper see-saws as it falls, the strip peels and flops with weight, domes inflate with a small overshoot as they leave the roller, squash on impact and pop in a fast ripple; the two engineers move on twos like printed puppets; one long held silence before the drop.
brief.typography: DIN Condensed only, printed into the world: the calendar year, figure captions under the two engineers like a magazine plate, price tags struck through in coral, stencil on the machine's crate base, the company name printed on a shipping label; captions are narrow condensed caps on torn newsprint slips.
brief.material: Theme offset: newsprint paper, teal surface ink for the wallpaper and the sheet, darker teal Ben-Day screens for shadow, near-black ink keylines, coral only for the reveal (1957, the names, Sealed Air); paper grain multiplied over everything.
brief.transitions: Every change rides the sheet: the flopped strip drapes over the engineers and is pulled off to reveal their workshop; the bubbled sheet runs down out of the roller and lands rolled in a shop rack; the unwanted roll is stretched into a greenhouse; the torn greenhouse sheet blows across the lens and lands wrapped around the computer; a dive into one bubble opens onto the original wall.
brief.sound: Physical foley only: a pop for every bubble that bursts, paper flutter and a floorboard tap for the calendar, a long cloth flop, roller creaks and soft puffs as domes inflate, swishes as other rolls sell, a pen strike, a tear and wind for the greenhouse, chain clank, one heavy thump and a ripple of pops on the drop; the music cuts out for the beat before the drop.

music.caption: late 1950s lounge exotica, tremolo electric guitar, bongos and shaker, soft Hammond organ chords, upright bass, playful and slightly comic, sparse opening, light cha-cha groove builds, a sudden stop, then a bright full finish, instrumental

brief.payoff: The drop: the wrapped tape drive falls onto the dock in silence, the bottom row of bubbles bursts in a ripple of pops, it bounces, settles and its reels quietly turn; then one bubble opens back onto the 1957 wall, where the engineers are still under their flopped strip.
